section: More than sixty years of optimal stopping

More than sixty years of optimal stopping
The secretary problem developed from a recreational question into a major model in optimal stopping, applied probability, decision theory, economics, and online algorithms.

title: Interactive Simulations
text:
What the experiments show
The simulations illustrate three important facts:

A nonrecord candidate cannot be the overall best.
Rejecting too few candidates provides insufficient information.
Rejecting too many candidates leaves too few opportunities to select a later record.

The optimal threshold balances these competing risks.
For large (n),
\[
r^\star\approx \frac{n}{e},
\qquad
P_n(r^\star)\approx\frac1e.
\]
Therefore, both the optimal rejection fraction and the maximum success probability approach approximately (37%).






NoteSimulation versus proof



Monte Carlo simulation provides numerical evidence, but it does not prove optimality. The exact probability formula and the backward-induction argument establish the mathematical result.

title: The Secretary Problem Atlas
text:
Why an atlas?
The secretary problem is not a single problem. It is a family of optimal-stopping models that changes according to the information available, the number of selections allowed, the objective, and the costs involved.
This website organizes those variants and makes their mathematical structure easier to compare.

title: The Classical Problem by Backward Induction
text:
We derive the optimal stopping rule from the Bellman recursion
\[
V_n=\max\{U_n,W_n\},
\]
where \(U_n\) is the value of stopping at stage \(n\) and \(W_n\) is the value of continuing.

title: The Classical Problem by Backward Induction
text:
We derive the optimal stopping rule from the Bellman recursion
\[
V_n=\max\{U_n,W_n\},
\]
where \(U_n\) is the value of stopping at stage \(n\) and \(W_n\) is the value of continuing.

title: The Classical Problem by Backward Induction
text:
1. The model
There are \(N\) candidates with distinct absolute ranks
\[
1,2,\ldots,N,
\]
where absolute rank \(1\) denotes the best candidate.
The candidates arrive in a uniformly random order. After interviewing candidate \(n\), the decision maker must either:

accept the candidate and stop, or
reject the candidate permanently and continue.

The objective is to maximize the probability of selecting the candidate of absolute rank \(1\).
Only relative ranks are observed. The absolute ranks of the candidates are not known during the selection process.

title: The Classical Problem by Backward Induction
text:
2. Relative ranks
Let \(X_n\) denote the absolute rank of the candidate interviewed at time \(n\). Define the relative rank
\[
R_n
=
1+\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}\mathbf{1}_{\{X_j<X_n\}}.
\]
Thus, \(R_n\) is the rank of candidate \(n\) among the first \(n\) candidates.
In particular,
$$
R_n=1 $$
means that candidate \(n\) is better than every candidate observed previouslylkj
sebelumnya. Such a candidate is called a record.






Important



A candidate can be the overall best only if they are a record when observed. Therefore, it is never optimal to accept a candidate with \(R_n>1\).

title: The Classical Problem by Backward Induction
text:
3. Uniformity oflkj of relative ranks

Theorem
Under a uniformly random arrival order,
\[
R_n\sim \operatorname{Uniform}\{1,\ldots,n\}.
\]
Moreover, the relative ranks
\[
R_1,R_2,\ldots,R_N
\]
are mutually independent.


Proof
Every permutation
\[
(X_1,\ldots,X_N)
\]
of the absolute ranks corresponds uniquely to a sequence of relative ranks satisfying
\[
R_n\in\{1,\ldots,n\}.
\]
Conversely, every sequence
\[
(r_1,\ldots,r_N),
\qquad
r_n\in\{1,\ldots,n\},
\]
determines a unique permutation.
There are
\[
1\cdot2\cdots N=N!
\]
possible relative-rank sequences, exactly matching the \(N!\) permutations of the absolute ranks.
Since every permutation is equally likely, every admissible relative-rank sequence has probability \(1/N!\). Therefore,
\[
\Pr(R_1=r_1,\ldots,R_N=r_N)
=
\prod_{n=1}^{N}\frac1n.
\]
It follows that the relative ranks are independent and
\[
\Pr(R_n=j)=\frac1n,
\qquad
j=1,\ldots,n.
\]
In particular,
\[
\Pr(R_n=1)=\frac1n.
\]

title: The Classical Problem by Backward Induction
text:
4. The reward from stopping
Suppose candidate \(n\) is a record. Define
\[
U_n
=
\Pr(X_n=1\mid R_n=1).
\]
This is the conditional probability of winning if we stop at stage \(n\).
Now,
\[
\Pr(X_n=1)=\frac1N,
\]
because the overall best candidate is equally likely to occupy any of the \(N\) positions. Also,
\[
\Pr(R_n=1)=\frac1n.
\]
Since \(X_n=1\) implies \(R_n=1\),
\[
\Pr(X_n=1,R_n=1)
=
\Pr(X_n=1)
=
\frac1N.
\]
Therefore,
\[
U_n
=
\frac{\Pr(X_n=1,R_n=1)}
     {\Pr(R_n=1)}
=
\frac{1/N}{1/n}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\boxed{U_n=\frac nN}.
\]
Thus, when candidate \(n\) is a record, accepting that candidate succeeds with probability \(n/N\).
If \(R_n>1\), the candidate cannot be the overall best, so the stopping reward is zero.

title: The Classical Problem by Backward Induction
text:
5. The continuation value
Let \(W_n\) denote the optimal probability of eventually selecting the overall best after candidate \(n\) has been rejected.
When candidate \(n\) is a record, define
\[
V_n=\max\{U_n,W_n\}.
\]
At stage \(n+1\), two cases are possible.

Case 1: Candidate \(n+1\) is a record
This occurs with probability
\[
\Pr(R_{n+1}=1)=\frac1{n+1}.
\]
The decision maker may then stop or continue. Therefore, the optimal value is
\[
V_{n+1}.
\]


Case 2: Candidate \(n+1\) is not a record
This occurs with probability
\[
\Pr(R_{n+1}>1)=\frac n{n+1}.
\]
A nonrecord cannot be the overall best, so it must be rejected. The remaining value is
\[
W_{n+1}.
\]
Combining the two cases gives the Bellman recursion
\[
\boxed{
W_n
=
\frac1{n+1}V_{n+1}
+
\frac n{n+1}W_{n+1}
}.
\]
Together with
\[
U_n=\frac nN
\]
and
\[
V_n=\max\{U_n,W_n\},
\]
we obtain the backward-induction system
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
U_n&=\frac nN,\\[4pt]
V_n&=\max\{U_n,W_n\},\\[4pt]
W_n&=
\frac1{n+1}V_{n+1}
+
\frac n{n+1}W_{n+1}.
\end{aligned}
}
\]

title: The Classical Problem by Backward Induction
text:
6. Terminal condition
At the final stage, there is no future candidate. Therefore,
\[
W_N=0.
\]
If candidate \(N\) is a record, that candidate must be the overall best. Hence,
\[
U_N=1.
\]
It follows that
\[
V_N=\max\{1,0\}=1.
\]
These terminal values allow the recursion to be evaluated backward from \(n=N\) to \(n=1\).

title: The Classical Problem by Backward Induction
text:
7. The optimal decision rule
When candidate \(n\) is a record, compare
\[
U_n=\frac nN
\]
with \(W_n\).
The optimal decision is
\[
\begin{cases}
\text{stop}, & U_n\geq W_n,\\[4pt]
\text{continue}, & U_n<W_n.
\end{cases}
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\boxed{
\text{accept candidate }n
\iff
R_n=1
\text{ and }
\frac nN\geq W_n.
}
\]
The stopping value \(U_n=n/N\) increases with \(n\). Meanwhile, the value of waiting decreases as the end of the observation horizon approaches. Therefore, the stopping and continuation values cross at a threshold.
Consequently, there is an integer \(r\) such that:

record candidates in positions \(1,\ldots,r\) are rejected;
the first record after position \(r\) is accepted.

The threshold rule is therefore derived from backward induction; it is not assumed in advance.

title: The Classical Problem by Backward Induction
text:
8. Complete example: \(N=10\)
We now solve the problem recursively for ten candidates.
The terminal values are
\[
W_{10}=0,
\qquad
U_{10}=1,
\qquad
V_{10}=1.
\]
At stage \(9\),
\[
W_9
=
\frac1{10}V_{10}
+
\frac9{10}W_{10}
=
\frac1{10}.
\]
Since
\[
U_9=\frac9{10}>\frac1{10}=W_9,
\]
we stop at a record in position \(9\).

Thus, the optimal rejection threshold is
\[
\boxed{r^\star=3}.
\]
The optimal success probability is

\boxed{
V_1
=

}
\]

title: The Classical Problem by Backward Induction
text:
9. Recovering the exact threshold formula
Suppose the first \(r\) candidates have been rejected. Under the threshold strategy, the overall best is selected if:

the overall best occurs at some position \(k>r\); and
the best among the first \(k-1\) candidates occurs among the first \(r\).

For a fixed \(k>r\),
\[
\Pr(X_k=1)=\frac1N.
\]
Conditional on the overall best appearing at position \(k\), the best candidate among positions \(1,\ldots,k-1\) is equally likely to occupy any of those \(k-1\) positions. Therefore,
\[
\Pr\left(
\text{best of the first }k-1
\text{ lies among the first }r
\right)
=
\frac r{k-1}.
\]
Hence,
\[
\Pr(\text{win with the best at }k)
=
\frac1N\frac r{k-1}.
\]
Summing over \(k=r+1,\ldots,N\) gives
\[
\boxed{
P_N(r)
=
\frac rN
\sum_{k=r+1}^{N}\frac1{k-1}
}.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\boxed{
P_N(r)
=
\frac rN
\sum_{j=r}^{N-1}\frac1j
}.
\]
This is precisely the continuation value \(W_r\) obtained after rejecting the first \(r\) candidates:
\[
\boxed{W_r=P_N(r)}.
\]

title: The Classical Problem by Backward Induction
text:
10. Characterization of the optimal threshold
The optimal threshold is the integer \(r^\star\) for which it is optimal to continue at \(r^\star\) but stop at the next record.
Continuing at stage \(r\) requires
\[
W_r\geq U_r.
\]
Using
\[
W_r
=
\frac rN\sum_{j=r}^{N-1}\frac1j
\]
and
\[
U_r=\frac rN,
\]
this condition becomes
\[
\sum_{j=r}^{N-1}\frac1j\geq 1.
\]
Stopping at a record in position \(r+1\) requires
\[
U_{r+1}\geq W_{r+1},
\]
which is equivalent to
\[
\sum_{j=r+1}^{N-1}\frac1j\leq 1.
\]
Therefore, the optimal threshold is characterized by
\[
\boxed{
\sum_{j=r^\star+1}^{N-1}\frac1j
\leq 1
\leq
\sum_{j=r^\star}^{N-1}\frac1j
}.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\boxed{
r^\star
=
\min\left\{
r:
\sum_{j=r+1}^{N-1}\frac1j\leq 1
\right\}.
}
\]
For \(N=10\),
\[
\sum_{j=4}^{9}\frac1j<1
\]
but
\[
\sum_{j=3}^{9}\frac1j>1.
\]
Therefore,
\[
r^\star=3.
\]

title: The Classical Problem by Backward Induction
text:
11. The asymptotic \(1/e\) rule
For large \(N\), the harmonic sum satisfies
\[
\sum_{j=r}^{N-1}\frac1j
\approx
\int_r^N\frac{dx}{x}
=
\log\left(\frac Nr\right).
\]
At the optimal threshold, this quantity is approximately \(1\). Thus,
\[
\log\left(\frac{N}{r^\star}\right)\approx 1.
\]
Exponentiating gives
\[
\frac{N}{r^\star}\approx e,
\]
and therefore
\[
\boxed{
\frac{r^\star}{N}\longrightarrow\frac1e
}.
\]
The optimal success probability satisfies
\[
P_N(r^\star)
=
\frac{r^\star}{N}
\sum_{j=r^\star}^{N-1}\frac1j.
\]
Since
\[
\frac{r^\star}{N}\longrightarrow\frac1e
\]
and the harmonic sum converges to \(1\),
\[
\boxed{
P_N(r^\star)\longrightarrow\frac1e
}.
\]
Thus, for a large number of candidates, the optimal strategy is approximately:

reject the first \(N/e\) candidates;
accept the first subsequent record.

Both the optimal rejection proportion and the limiting success probability approach
\[
\boxed{\frac1e\approx 0.367879}.
\]

title: The Classical Problem by Backward Induction
text:
12. Final result






TipOptimal classical secretary rule



For \(N\) candidates arriving in uniformly random order:

Determine the threshold \(r^\star\) from
\[
\sum_{j=r^\star+1}^{N-1}\frac1j
\leq 1
\leq
\sum_{j=r^\star}^{N-1}\frac1j.
\]
Reject the first \(r^\star\) candidates.
Accept the first later candidate whose relative rank is \(1\).

The rule follows from the recursion
\[
V_n=\max\{U_n,W_n\},
\]
where
\[
U_n=\frac nN
\]
and
\[
W_n
=
\frac1{n+1}V_{n+1}
+
\frac n{n+1}W_{n+1}.
\]
As \(N\to\infty\),
\[
\frac{r^\star}{N}\longrightarrow\frac1e,
\qquad
P_N(r^\star)\longrightarrow\frac1e.
\]

title: The Classical Problem by Backward Induction
text:
13. The backward-induction theorem
The preceding solution is an application of the general finite-horizon optimal stopping theorem (Chow, Robbins, and Siegmund 1971; Ferguson 2010; Shiryaev 2007).

Theorem
Let
\[
(\Omega,\mathcal F,\{\mathcal F_n\}_{n=1}^{N},\Pr)
\]
be a filtered probability space. Let
\[
U_1,U_2,\ldots,U_N
\]
be an integrable adapted reward process, where \(U_n\) is the reward obtained by stopping at time \(n\).
For each \(n\), let \(\mathcal T_n\) denote the set of stopping times taking values in
\[
\{n,n+1,\ldots,N\}.
\]
Define the value process by
\[
V_n
=
\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{\tau\in\mathcal T_n}
\operatorname E[U_\tau\mid\mathcal F_n].
\]
Then
\[
V_N=U_N
\]
and, for \(n=N-1,\ldots,1\),
\[
\boxed{
V_n
=
\max\left\{
U_n,
\operatorname E[V_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]
\right\}.
}
\]
If the continuation value is defined by
\[
W_n
=
\operatorname E[V_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n],
\]
then the recursion becomes
\[
\boxed{V_n=\max\{U_n,W_n\}}.
\]
Moreover, subject to forced stopping at time \(N\), the stopping time
\[
\boxed{
\tau^\star
=
\inf\{n:U_n\geq W_n\}
}
\]
is optimal.


Proof
At time \(N\), stopping is mandatory. Therefore,
\[
V_N=U_N.
\]
Suppose that \(V_{n+1}\) is the optimal value from time \(n+1\) onward.
At time \(n\), the decision maker has two possible actions:

stop immediately and receive \(U_n\);
continue and receive the conditional expected optimal future value
\[
W_n
=
\operatorname E[V_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n].
\]

An optimal decision selects the action with the larger value. Hence,
\[
V_n=\max\{U_n,W_n\}.
\]
Starting from \(V_N=U_N\) and repeating this argument for
\[
n=N-1,N-2,\ldots,1
\]
determines the entire value process by backward induction.
At every time \(n\), stopping when \(U_n\geq W_n\) selects an action attaining the value \(V_n\). Therefore, the first time at which this inequality holds is an optimal stopping time:
\[
\tau^\star
=
\inf\{n:U_n\geq W_n\}.
\]
This proves the result. \(\square\)


Application to the classical secretary problem
In the classical secretary problem, a nonrecord candidate cannot be the overall best and therefore has stopping value zero.
If candidate \(n\) is a record, the immediate stopping value is
\[
U_n=\frac nN.
\]
The continuation value is
\[
W_n
=
\operatorname E[V_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n].
\]
Because
\[
\Pr(R_{n+1}=1)=\frac1{n+1},
\]
we obtain
\[
W_n
=
\frac1{n+1}V_{n+1}
+
\frac n{n+1}W_{n+1}.
\]
Consequently, the secretary-problem recursion
\[
V_n=\max\{U_n,W_n\}
\]
is a direct specialization of the finite-horizon backward-induction theorem.

title: The Classical Problem by Backward Induction
text:
Sources
The classical secretary problem and its full-information extensions are developed by Gilbert and Mosteller (1966). Historical details are discussed by Ferguson (1989).
The general theory of finite-horizon optimal stopping and backward induction is treated by Chow, Robbins, and Siegmund (1971), Ferguson (2010), and Shiryaev (2007).
The notation and presentation used here follow the optimal-stopping framework employed in the research and dissertation work of José A. Islas.

title: The Classical Secretary Problem
text:
Observe candidates sequentially, reject an initial sample, and then select the first candidate who is better than everyone previously observed.
The classical model and its principal extensions are treated by (Gilbert and Mosteller 1966; Freeman 1983), while its historical development is discussed by Ferguson (1989).

title: The Classical Secretary Problem
text:
The decision problem
Suppose (n) candidates arrive in a uniformly random order.
After observing each candidate, you must either:

accept the candidate and stop, or
reject the candidate permanently and continue.

The objective is to select the best candidate among all (n) candidates.

title: The Classical Secretary Problem
text:
The threshold strategy
Choose an integer (r) with (0 r < n).

Reject the first (r) candidates.
Record the best candidate observed during that period.
Accept the first later candidate who is better than that recorded candidate.
If nobody exceeds the recorded candidate, the selection fails.

title: The Classical Secretary Problem
text:
Exact success probability
For (r ), the probability of selecting the best candidate is
\[
P_n(r)
=
\frac{r}{n}
\sum_{k=r+1}^{n}\frac{1}{k-1}.
\]
The optimal threshold is the integer (r) that maximizes (P_n(r)).
For large (n),
\[
r^\star \approx \frac{n}{e},
\qquad
P_n(r^\star)\approx \frac{1}{e}.
\]
Thus, approximately (37%) of the candidates are observed and rejected before selection begins.

title: About
text:
The Secretary Problem Atlas is a free, open-access educational and science-communication project created by José Ángel Islas Anguiano at Universidad Autónoma de Sinaloa. Its purpose is to make the mathematics, history, and applications of optimal stopping and secretary problems accessible to students, educators, researchers, and the general public.
The Atlas combines intuitive explanations, mathematical derivations, interactive visualizations, historical context, and research references. No registration or payment is required.

title: References
text:
This bibliography supports the mathematical explanations, historical notes, and interactive experiments presented in The Secretary Problem Atlas.


The initial collection includes foundational work on the classical secretary problem, full-information models, historical development, extensions, and related optimal-stopping principles.
As the Atlas grows, this database will be expanded to include literature on:

multiple-choice secretary problems,
selecting the second-best candidate,
generalized top-(m) objectives,
full-information best-choice models,
duration problems,
interview costs and rewards,
unknown numbers of candidates,
rank-dependent payoffs.
